results.title: Do women make better spies?
results.description: Forget James Bond! Female spies are taking over everyone’s imagination ever since the Nvidia co-founder and an alleged Chinese spy’s affair came to light. Authors, ex-intelligence officers, and filmmakers tell us a good female spy’s skills depend on motivation and their ability to spot and manipulate vulnerability.
creator: mid-day

results.title: The oldest trap in the spy’s book
results.description: Wars today are fought with drones, malware, and artificial intelligence. Yet two recent news reports show that the spy’s most dependable weapon is still the oldest one: a flattering stranger and a man who wants to be admired. In New Delhi, a police chargesheet accuses a serving Indian Air Force Wing Commander, arrested under the Official Secrets Act, of passing classified details to a suspected Pakistani intelligence operative. The leaked material allegedly included secret war plans, the strength of a covert drone unit, and fighter deployments in Leh. Police say the two chatted on WhatsApp for months until the officer was caught carrying a smartphone inside his office. Shockingly, he allegedly traded pages of a secret war plan in exchange for explicit photographs, and even installed spyware on the phones of five subordinates. Around the same time in the United States, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned following reports of an affair with Alice Huang, a woman of no relation whom American officials suspect was passing information to the Chinese government. While Beijing has dismissed the claims and it remains unclear what, if anything, was leaked, intelligence experts point out that a secret relationship at that level is a major security risk on its own. Honey trapping is one of the oldest tricks in espionage. Sometimes targets are blackmailed after being lured into compromising situations; other times, an intelligence agency notices a natural relationship developing and pressures the partner to spy. History shows that even trained professionals are not immune. In the 1960s, for instance, French diplomat Bernard Boursicot fell into a secret romance with a Peking opera singer in China. Chinese intelligence agents eventually told him he could only keep seeing his partner if he handed over embassy documents, and he complied for years. In today’s digital age, this threat has spread far beyond high-profile officials and corporate leaders. With social media and encrypted messaging apps, cybercriminals now run honey traps on an industrial scale, targeting ordinary citizens. Fake profiles, flattering messages, and staged video calls are routinely used to lure unsuspecting people into compromising positions, leaving common victims trapped in endless cycles of financial extortion and public humiliation. Such traps succeed because they exploit basic human psychology. The German philosopher Friedrich Nietzsche never wrote about espionage, yet he understood how easily people are drawn into dangerous situations when they lower their guard. As he famously warned, “When you gaze long into an abyss, the abyss gazes back.” A honey trap is simply that abyss dressed up as affection. Victims are rarely fools; they are often capable men who trust their own judgment too much. Men in top positions are usually surrounded by obedience, not genuine admiration, so a stranger who makes them feel truly appreciated can quickly become a blind spot. These incidents prove a vital lesson: beyond high intelligence and sharp professional skills, moral integrity is equally important for anyone holding a high post. Rank and cleverness offer no protection when personal discipline fails. For those in positions of authority, caution is the best defence. Unexplained attention and sudden flattery from strangers must always be viewed with suspicion. Official work should never enter private chats, as a document sent over WhatsApp is beyond your control the moment you press send, and intimate photographs must never be exchanged since they become permanent tools for blackmail. Above all, remember that any relationship you have to hide from your organisation is already a serious liability. Shame only works in secret, so reporting a suspicious approach early allows your institution to manage the risk before it turns into a disaster. The write is a Kashmir based academic and teaches Political Science in the Higher Education Department of J&K.
creator: sajad padder

results.title: Ukraine Says Starshield Restrictions Persist, Hampering Drone Defenses
results.description: Ukraine says restrictions affecting its use of SpaceX’s Starshield satellite communications system remain widespread, hampering the military’s ability to intercept Russian jet-powered attack drones near the front line and giving Moscow additional opportunities to strike Ukrainian targets.

results.title: Kushner wants direct Russia-Europe talks in Ukraine peace push - Sat, 14 Nov 2026 PST
results.description: Jared Kushner, the U.S. president’s son-in-law who has been serving as a negotiator with Russia and Ukraine, said the Trump administration wants to see direct talks between Moscow and U.S. allies in Europe.
